stem: How is 'blindness' defined in terms of its effect on daily living?
options: The complete or almost complete loss of vision that cannot be corrected by glasses, contact lenses, medication, or surgery, to the extent that it significantly impairs a person's ability to perform activities of daily living using sight alone
Any reduction in visual acuity that can be fully corrected with spectacles
A temporary reduction in vision lasting less than 24 hours
A condition that affects only the ability to read small print

stem: According to the WHO Classification of Visual Impairment, what visual acuity range in the better eye defines Normal/mild impairment?
options: Less than 6/18 to 6/60
Less than 6/60 to 3/60
Less than 3/60

stem: According to the WHO Classification, what visual acuity range in the better eye defines Moderate visual impairment?
options: Less than 6/18 to 6/60
Less than 3/60 to no light perception
Less than 6/60 to 3/60

stem: According to the WHO Classification, what visual acuity range in the better eye defines Severe visual impairment?
options: Less than 6/60 to 3/60
Less than 6/18 to 6/60
No light perception only

stem: According to the WHO Classification, blindness is defined as visual acuity of less than 3/60, OR which alternative criterion?
options: A visual field of less than 10 degrees around central fixation
A visual field of more than 90 degrees around central fixation
Any visual acuity below 6/6
Inability to read newsprint at 40 cm

stem: The term 'low vision' is commonly used to describe which category of visual impairment?
options: Moderate visual impairment, which is worse than 6/18 but better than blindness, even with best correction
Total and complete loss of all light perception
Visual acuity of exactly 6/6 in both eyes
A visual field defect affecting only peripheral vision with normal central acuity

stem: Blindness can be classified by avoidability. What does 'preventable blindness' refer to?
options: Blindness that could have been avoided through health promotion and prevention, such as trachoma, vitamin A deficiency, ophthalmia neonatorum, and trauma
Blindness that is always curable once it occurs
Blindness that occurs only in adults over age 60
Blindness caused exclusively by genetic mutations

stem: What does 'curable/treatable blindness' refer to, under the classification of blindness by avoidability?
options: Blindness that is reversible with timely treatment, such as cataract and some cases of corneal opacity or refractive error
Blindness that can never be reversed under any circumstances
Blindness present from birth in all cases
Blindness that affects only one eye

stem: 'Avoidable blindness' is best described as the sum of which two categories?
options: Preventable blindness and curable/treatable blindness
Congenital blindness and acquired blindness
Unilateral blindness and bilateral blindness
Moderate visual impairment and severe visual impairment

stem: Avoidable blindness is considered the major target of which type of programme?
options: Blindness-prevention programmes
Programmes for congenital heart disease screening
General nutrition programmes unrelated to eye health
Maternal mortality reduction programmes

stem: 'Unavoidable blindness' refers to blindness that cannot currently be prevented or cured, giving which example?
options: Advanced optic atrophy or some inherited retinal dystrophies
Cataract diagnosed early in a community eye camp
Refractive error correctable with spectacles
Conjunctivitis treated promptly at a primary health centre

stem: Blindness can also be classified by onset. What is 'congenital blindness'?
options: Blindness present at or shortly after birth
Blindness that develops after the age of 60 only
Blindness that results exclusively from trauma in adulthood
Blindness that is always temporary and resolves spontaneously

stem: What is 'acquired blindness', as distinguished from congenital blindness?
options: Blindness developing later in life from disease, trauma, or degeneration
Blindness present at birth only
Blindness caused solely by inherited chromosomal abnormalities
Blindness that cannot be classified by onset at all

stem: Blindness can also be classified by laterality. What distinguishes 'unilateral' from 'bilateral' blindness?
options: Unilateral blindness affects one eye, while bilateral blindness affects both eyes
Unilateral blindness is always congenital, while bilateral blindness is always acquired
Unilateral blindness is always curable, while bilateral blindness is always unavoidable
There is no distinction; the terms are interchangeable

stem: The Nigeria National Blindness and Visual Impairment Survey, conducted over 2005 to 2007, is notable for which feature?
options: It was the largest population-based eye survey in the country, examining over 13,500 adults aged 40 years and above
It examined only children under five years of age
It was conducted exclusively in urban hospital settings
It surveyed fewer than 500 participants nationwide

stem: According to the Nigeria National Blindness and Visual Impairment Survey, what was the estimated prevalence of blindness (presenting vision) among adults aged 40 years and above?
options: 4.2%, translating to an estimated 1.13 million blind adults
0.2%, translating to fewer than 50,000 blind adults
25%, translating to over 10 million blind adults
4.2% among children under five only

stem: In which geopolitical zone of Nigeria was blindness prevalence found to be HIGHEST, also carrying the largest share of the country's blind population?
options: The North-West geopolitical zone
The South-West geopolitical zone only
The South-South geopolitical zone only
The Federal Capital Territory exclusively

stem: Blindness prevalence in Nigeria was found to be significantly higher among which groups?
options: Women, illiterate persons, and people in poorer households
Only men with tertiary education
Only children under the age of five
Only residents of the wealthiest urban households

stem: More recent state-level Rapid Assessment of Avoidable Blindness (RAAB) surveys, such as in Kogi State, found blindness prevalence in which range, confirming the burden remained substantial?
options: Around 3.0% to 3.7%
Around 0.1% to 0.5%
Around 25% to 30%
Around 50% to 60%

stem: Nigeria's National Eye Health Programme more recently cited an estimated national blindness figure of how many people?
options: About 1.3 million people currently blind
About 13,000 people currently blind
About 130 million people currently blind
About 1,300 people currently blind

stem: According to the National Blindness and Visual Impairment Survey, approximately what percentage of blindness in Nigeria is avoidable (preventable or treatable)?
options: Approximately 84%
Approximately 8%
Approximately 50%
Approximately 100%, with no exceptions

stem: What is the SINGLE leading cause of blindness in Nigeria, accounting for roughly 43% of cases?
options: Cataract
Glaucoma
Trachoma
Onchocerciasis

stem: What is the leading cause of IRREVERSIBLE blindness in Nigeria, accounting for roughly 16.7% of cases?
options: Glaucoma
Cataract
Uncorrected refractive error
Corneal opacity

stem: What does 'uncorrected aphakia', a cause of blindness in Nigeria, specifically refer to?
options: An unoperated or complicated cataract surgery performed without a replacement lens
A refractive error correctable by simple reading glasses
A tumour of the orbit in adults
A genetic condition present at birth

stem: Corneal opacity/scarring, a cause of blindness in Nigeria accounting for roughly 7.9% of cases, most commonly results from which causes?
options: Trauma, infection, or harmful traditional eye medicine
Normal ageing alone, with no other contributing factor
Vitamin overdose exclusively
Excessive screen time alone

stem: In the same Nigerian survey population, uncorrected refractive error, while rarely a cause of outright blindness, is responsible for the majority of which condition?
options: Moderate visual impairment
Severe systemic hypertension
Childhood malnutrition
Congenital heart disease

stem: Globally, which condition is considered the single commonest cause of visual impairment worldwide?
options: Uncorrected refractive error
Retinoblastoma
Ocular surface squamous neoplasia
Ophthalmia neonatorum

stem: Which infectious cause of blindness is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, spread by flies and poor hygiene, leading to inward-turned eyelashes that scratch the cornea?
options: Trachoma
Onchocerciasis
Ophthalmia neonatorum
Retinoblastoma

stem: What term describes the inward-turning of the eyelashes caused by repeated trachoma infection, which then scratches the cornea?
options: Trichiasis
Leukocoria
Phthisis bulbi
Xerophthalmia

stem: Onchocerciasis ('river blindness') is caused by which organism?
options: The filarial worm Onchocerca volvulus
Chlamydia trachomatis
Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Vitamin A deficiency

stem: Onchocerciasis is transmitted by which vector, which breeds in fast-flowing rivers?
options: The blackfly (Simulium)
The mosquito (Anopheles)
The tsetse fly
The housefly (Musca domestica)

stem: Corneal ulcers, as a cause of eye problems, most often follow which of the following?
options: Trauma, exposure, or scratches from unorthodox/traditional eye medicines
Routine use of prescribed spectacles
Adequate vitamin A intake
Immunization against rubella

stem: Ophthalmia neonatorum is usually caused by which maternal infections transmitted during delivery?
options: Maternal gonococcal or chlamydial infection
Maternal vitamin A deficiency
Maternal diabetes mellitus
Maternal iron-deficiency anaemia

stem: If left untreated, ophthalmia neonatorum can rapidly progress to cause which serious complication?
options: Corneal perforation and blindness
Complete resolution without any treatment required
Improved visual acuity compared to baseline
A benign, self-limiting rash with no ocular involvement

stem: Vitamin A deficiency (VAD), as a nutritional cause of eye problems, can lead to night blindness, conjunctival/corneal xerosis, Bitot's spots, and which severe complication?
options: Keratomalacia (corneal melting)
Retinoblastoma
Pterygium
Diabetic retinopathy

stem: Vitamin A deficiency and its ocular complications are especially significant in which population group?
options: Malnourished children under the age of five
Adults over the age of 80 exclusively
Pregnant women in the third trimester exclusively
Healthy, well-nourished adolescents

stem: Cataract, a degenerative and age-related condition, refers to which pathological process?
options: Clouding of the lens
Clouding of the cornea only
Scarring of the conjunctiva
Inflammation of the eyelid margin

stem: Besides being strongly age-related, cataract can also be which of the following?
options: Congenital, traumatic, or secondary to diabetes or steroid use
Exclusively inherited, with no other possible cause
Caused only by excessive reading
Entirely reversible without any surgical intervention

stem: Glaucoma is best described as which pathological process?
options: Progressive optic nerve damage, usually associated with raised intraocular pressure
Clouding of the lens due to ageing
A wing-shaped growth on the corneal surface
An infection of the conjunctiva caused by bacteria

stem: Why is glaucoma sometimes referred to as 'the silent thief of sight'?
options: Because it often remains asymptomatic until the disease is advanced
Because it always causes sudden, severe pain from the very first symptom
Because it exclusively affects children under five years old
Because it is always accompanied by a visible white pupillary reflex

stem: Diabetic retinopathy results from which underlying process?
options: Damage to retinal blood vessels from long-standing, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus
A congenital abnormality of the optic nerve present at birth
An allergic reaction to pollen and dust
A bacterial infection of the eyelid margin

stem: Ocular trauma, as a cause of blindness, commonly arises from which activities, particularly in farming communities?
options: Accidents, domestic violence, sports, and agricultural tools
Routine antenatal check-ups
Scheduled eye screening clinics
Vitamin A supplementation programmes

stem: Retinopathy of prematurity, a congenital/genetic category cause of blindness, is specifically associated with which exposure in preterm or low-birth-weight babies?
options: Uncontrolled oxygen therapy
Excessive vitamin A supplementation
Maternal rubella infection in the third trimester only
Routine newborn eye prophylaxis with antibiotic ointment

stem: Which harmful practice involves instilling breast milk, urine, or plant/herbal concoctions into the eye for 'cleansing' or treatment of red eye, and is a well-documented cause of corneal ulceration and blindness in Nigeria?
options: Harmful traditional and self-medication eye practices
Standard pharmacological eye drop therapy prescribed by an ophthalmologist
Routine use of artificial tears for dry eye
Use of UV-protective sunglasses

stem: Retinoblastoma, a tumour affecting children, presents classically with which finding?
options: A white pupillary reflex, described as 'leukocoria' or 'cat's eye reflex'
A red, painful eye with purulent discharge
A wing-shaped growth on the cornea
Complete absence of the eyeball at birth

stem: Ocular surface squamous neoplasia, a tumour affecting adults, is particularly associated with which infection?
options: HIV infection
Vitamin A deficiency
Onchocerciasis
Ophthalmia neonatorum

stem: In the Nigerian context, cataract is described as the single leading cause of blindness, with a large backlog of untreated cases due to which combination of factors?
options: Poor awareness, cost, distance to surgical services, and fear of surgery
Universal free access to surgery with no remaining backlog
Excess surgical capacity with too few patients to treat
A complete absence of any surgical treatment option

stem: In the Nigerian context, glaucoma is described as the second leading cause of blindness, noted for which clinical course in populations of African descent?
options: A more aggressive course, often asymptomatic until advanced
A course that is always mild and self-limiting
A course that exclusively affects people under 10 years old
A course that resolves spontaneously without any treatment

stem: In the Nigerian context, uncorrected refractive error is described as the leading cause of which category of visual impairment?
options: Moderate visual impairment
Total, irreversible blindness in the majority of cases
Congenital blindness exclusively
Unilateral traumatic blindness exclusively

stem: Trachoma, as an eye condition in the Nigerian context, is noted to be endemic in which part of the country, and is targeted for elimination as a neglected tropical disease?
options: Some northern states
Exclusively the Niger Delta region
Exclusively Lagos State
Exclusively the Federal Capital Territory

stem: Onchocerciasis (river blindness) in Nigeria is endemic along river basins in which parts of the country?
options: North-Central, South-South, and South-East Nigeria
Exclusively the extreme North-East
Exclusively coastal Lagos
Exclusively the Federal Capital Territory

stem: Onchocerciasis is controlled in endemic Nigerian communities through which community-based strategy?
options: Community-directed treatment with ivermectin (CDTI)
Mandatory enucleation of affected eyes
Universal corneal transplantation
Annual mass vitamin A megadose campaigns exclusively

stem: Vitamin A deficiency/xerophthalmia, as a significant cause of childhood blindness in Nigeria, is linked to which factors?
options: Poverty, poor complementary feeding, and low uptake of vitamin A supplementation
Excessive maternal vitamin A intake during pregnancy
Universal, complete vitamin A supplementation coverage nationwide
Only children from the wealthiest households

stem: Pterygium, a common eye condition in Nigeria, is best described as which pathological finding?
options: A wing-shaped fibrovascular growth on the cornea associated with chronic ultraviolet light and dust exposure
A clouding of the lens associated with ageing
A tumour of the orbit associated with HIV infection
A congenital abnormality of the eyelid present at birth

stem: Allergic conjunctivitis, a common presenting complaint at the primary health centre level in Nigeria, is particularly worsened by which environmental factors?
options: Dust and harmattan
Cold, humid weather only
Excessive hand hygiene
High-altitude living only

stem: Ophthalmia neonatorum is still seen in Nigeria due to which gaps in care?
options: Poor antenatal screening and treatment of maternal sexually transmitted infections, and inadequate eye prophylaxis at birth
Excessive, unnecessary antibiotic eye prophylaxis given to every newborn
Universal, complete antenatal STI screening with no remaining gaps
Overuse of vitamin A supplementation in neonates

stem: What is Primary Eye Care (PEC)?
options: The integration of essential eye health services into the general primary health care system
A specialist tertiary hospital service available only in major cities
A programme limited strictly to cataract surgery
A private insurance scheme covering only spectacles

stem: Primary Eye Care (PEC) aims to deliver promotive, preventive, and basic curative eye care as close as possible to which setting?
options: Where people live and work
Only within specialist tertiary hospitals located in state capitals
Only within private ophthalmology clinics
Only within research laboratories

stem: Primary Eye Care is usually delivered by which non-specialist category of health worker, with a functional referral pathway to secondary and tertiary levels?
options: Community health officers, primary health care nurses, and community health extension workers (CHEWs)
Consultant ophthalmologists exclusively
Pharmaceutical company representatives exclusively
Hospital administrators exclusively

stem: The WHO African Region has developed a package of Primary Eye Care interventions built around which core components?
options: Health promotion, screening/early detection, basic treatment, and prompt referral of sight-threatening cases
Advanced laser surgery performed at the community level by lay volunteers
Exclusively the distribution of free spectacles with no further services
Exclusively hospital-based tertiary interventions with no community component

stem: The concept of Primary Eye Care underlies which national programme and global initiative?
options: The National Eye Health Policy and the VISION 2020: The Right to Sight programme
The National Blood Transfusion Policy exclusively
The National Immunization Policy exclusively
The National Malaria Elimination Programme exclusively

stem: Both the National Eye Health Policy and VISION 2020 depend on which category of workers to identify eye problems early, educate, and refer appropriately?
options: Nurses and other primary health care workers
Only tertiary hospital consultants
Only traditional birth attendants
Only pharmaceutical sales representatives

stem: Which risk factor is noted to be markedly higher among the poorest households, affecting both cataract surgical coverage and spectacle wear?
options: Poverty
High household income
Advanced university education
Urban residence with easy access to eye clinics

stem: Gender is identified as a risk factor for blindness in Nigeria because women bear a disproportionate burden of which condition, often linked to poorer access to surgical services?
options: Cataract-related blindness
Congenital glaucoma exclusively
Retinoblastoma exclusively
Ophthalmia neonatorum exclusively

stem: Rural residence is identified as a risk factor for blindness in Nigeria primarily because of which barrier?
options: Geographic and economic barriers to reaching eye care facilities
An oversupply of ophthalmologists in rural areas
Free, unlimited transportation to urban eye hospitals
Mandatory annual eye screening in every rural village

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A 65-year-old farmer from a rural North-Western Nigerian community presents with gradually worsening bilateral blurred vision over two years. Visual acuity in the better eye is 2/60. He reports no pain and attributes the change to 'old age,' never having sought care due to cost and distance to the nearest eye clinic. Which classification and likely leading cause BEST fit this presentation?
options: He meets the WHO criterion for blindness (less than 3/60), and given the epidemiological pattern described, cataract is the single most likely leading cause, with poverty and distance identified as key risk factors
He is classified as having normal visual acuity, since 2/60 falls within the 6/6 to 6/18 range
He has unavoidable blindness, since all blindness in elderly farmers is classified as unavoidable by definition
His presentation is diagnostic of retinoblastoma, which is a childhood tumour

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A community health extension worker (CHEW) at a rural primary health centre sees a child under five with night blindness, dry conjunctiva, and small foamy white spots on the conjunctiva. The mother reports the child's diet is mostly starchy staples with little variety. Which diagnosis and health system response BEST fit this case?
options: Vitamin A deficiency (xerophthalmia) with Bitot's spots; this falls within the scope of Primary Eye Care, requiring prompt supplementation and dietary counselling, with referral if keratomalacia develops
Glaucoma, requiring immediate laser surgery only available at tertiary level
Retinopathy of prematurity, which only affects preterm neonates and is unrelated to this child's age or diet
Pterygium, which requires no nutritional intervention of any kind

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A newborn develops bilateral purulent eye discharge and swollen eyelids on day 3 of life. The mother's antenatal records show no documented screening or treatment for sexually transmitted infections. Which condition is MOST likely, and what is the urgency of referral?
options: Ophthalmia neonatorum, most likely from maternal gonococcal or chlamydial infection; this is an emergency requiring prompt treatment and referral, since delay can rapidly cause corneal perforation and blindness
Allergic conjunctivitis from harmattan dust, which can safely be observed for several weeks before any treatment
Congenital cataract, which requires no treatment until school age
A normal newborn finding requiring no further action or referral

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A 40-year-old woman living along a river basin in South-South Nigeria presents with intensely itchy skin nodules and progressive visual field loss, in a community where many neighbours have similar symptoms and where mass ivermectin distribution has not reached in recent years. Which condition and causative organism BEST fit this picture?
options: Onchocerciasis (river blindness), caused by the filarial worm Onchocerca volvulus and transmitted by the blackfly Simulium, which breeds in the fast-flowing river nearby
Trachoma, caused by Chlamydia trachomatis and spread by flies in dry, dusty northern communities
Diabetic retinopathy, caused by long-standing poorly controlled diabetes mellitus unrelated to her location
Ocular surface squamous neoplasia, associated with HIV infection rather than river exposure

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A primary health care nurse at a rural clinic is asked to design a basic eye care service for her catchment population, in line with national eye health policy. Which combination of activities BEST reflects the core components of Primary Eye Care she should include?
options: Health promotion and education, screening and early detection of common conditions, basic treatment within her scope of practice, and a functional referral pathway to secondary and tertiary eye care for sight-threatening cases
Performing cataract surgery herself at the primary health centre without any referral pathway
Referring every single patient directly to a tertiary teaching hospital regardless of severity, with no local screening or treatment
Distributing spectacles only, with no health promotion, screening, or referral component
